items.readable_text:
Content:
In this topic, we will use Fourier series to solve boundary value problems with periodic forcing functions.

Content:
As before, we consider a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function [MATH: f(x)], for which the general solution can be written as
[MATH: y=y_c+y_p,]
where [MATH: y_c] solves the homogeneous equation and [MATH: y_p] is a particular solution.

Content:
The main ideas are similar to those of solving IVPs:

Content:
- we choose the correct form of the series for the particular solution [MATH: y_p], and then
- use boundary conditions at the endpoints to determine the constants in the homogeneous part [MATH: y_c] of the solution.

Content:
When [MATH: f(x)] is periodic, we often look for [MATH: y_p] as a Fourier series on a symmetric interval [MATH: [-L,L].]

Content:
Recall that for an equation of the form [MATH: y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)] with no (damping) [MATH: y'] term, the particular solution inherits the parity of [MATH: f(x)]:

Content:
- If [MATH: f] is even, then its Fourier series contains only cosine terms.
- If [MATH: f] is odd, then its Fourier series contains only sine terms.

Content:
For example, consider the boundary value problem
[MATH: y''+5y=f(x)]
on [MATH: [-2,2]], where [MATH: f] is [MATH: 4]-periodic and odd. We want the appropriate Fourier series form for a particular solution [MATH: y_p].

Content:
Because [MATH: f] is [MATH: 4]-periodic on [MATH: [-2,2]], we have [MATH: L=2], so the Fourier basis on this interval is
[MATH: \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).]

Content:
Next, since [MATH: f] is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. Since the equation has no [MATH: y'] term, the particular solution inherits the same parity and is also odd.

Content:
Therefore, the appropriate form for [MATH: y_p] is a sine series:
[MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).]

sections.normalized_html: Consider the boundary value problem [MATH: y''+8y=f(x)] on [MATH: [-3,3]], where [MATH: f] is [MATH: 6]-periodic and even. What Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution [MATH: y_p?]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the boundary value problem
[MATH: y''+8y=f(x)]
on [MATH: [-3,3]], where [MATH: f] is [MATH: 6]-periodic and even. What Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution [MATH: y_p?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Because [MATH: f] is [MATH: 6]-periodic on [MATH: [-3,3]], we have [MATH: L=3], so Fourier series on this interval use the basis [MATH: \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right).]

Next, since [MATH: f] is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no [MATH: y'] (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for [MATH: y_p] is a cosine series: [MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right)]

Recall that we are considering a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function [MATH: f(x)], for which the general solution can be written as
[MATH: y=y_c+y_p,]
where [MATH: y_c] solves the homogeneous equation and [MATH: y_p] is a particular solution.

Content:
There are many types of boundary conditions (including mixed or Robin-type conditions), but in this lesson, we will focus on the two simplest cases:

Content:
- Dirichlet conditions (values of [MATH: y] are specified):
[MATH: y(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=\beta]
- Neumann conditions (values of [MATH: y'] are specified):
[MATH: y'(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=\beta]

Content:
A key simplification is possible if we choose our particular solution [MATH: y_p] to satisfy the corresponding homogeneous boundary conditions. For any given [MATH: f(x),] it is always possible to find such a [MATH: y_p].
This drastically simplifies the computations, as the boundary conditions then determine the constants in [MATH: y_c] directly.

Content:
- Dirichlet-type simplification: If we choose the forcing so that
[MATH: y_p(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p(b)=0,]
then
[MATH: y(a)=y_c(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=y_c(b),]
so we can solve for the constants in [MATH: y_c] using only the homogeneous solution.
- Neumann-type simplification: If we choose the forcing so that
[MATH: y_p'(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p'(b)=0,]
then
[MATH: y'(a)=y_c'(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=y_c'(b),]
so the derivative conditions determine the constants in [MATH: y_c] directly.

Consider the boundary value problem [MATH: y''+2y=f(x), \qquad y'(0)=0,\quad y'(1)=-5] where [MATH: f(x)] is [MATH: 2]-periodic and even. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution [MATH: y_p] of the differential equation.

Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function [MATH: f(x)] is chosen such that the particular solution [MATH: y_p] satisfies [MATH: y_p'(0) = 0] and [MATH: y_p'(1) = 0.] [MATH: (1)/(xxx)?(1)/(xxx)]

Consider the boundary value problem

where [MATH: f(x)] is [MATH: 2]-periodic and even. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution [MATH: y_p] of the differential equation.

Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function [MATH: f(x)] is chosen such that the particular solution [MATH: y_p] satisfies [MATH: y_p'(0) = 0] and [MATH: y_p'(1) = 0.]
[MATH: (1)/(xxx)?(1)/(xxx)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We write the solution as [MATH: y=y_c+y_p], where [MATH: y_c] solves the homogeneous equation and [MATH: y_p] is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation [MATH: y''+2y=0.] Its general solution is [MATH: y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sin(\sqrt{2}x).]

Computing the derivative, we get [MATH: y'(x)=-A\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sqrt{2}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+y_p'(x).]

Now, we use the hint. Since [MATH: y_p'(0)=0] and [MATH: y_p'(1)=0], we have [MATH: y'(0)=y_c'(0)\qquad\text{and}\qquad y'(1)=y_c'(1).]

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

  • Use [MATH: y'(0)=0{:}] [MATH: y^{′}(0)|= 0 + Bsqrt(2)(1) + y_{p}^{′}(0); 0|= Bsqrt(2) + 0; B|= 0] So, [MATH: y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x).]

  • Use [MATH: y'(1)=-5] with [MATH: B=0{:}] [MATH: y^{′}(1)|= − Asqrt(2)\sin (sqrt(2)) + y_{p}^{′}(1); − 5|= − Asqrt(2)\sin (sqrt(2)) + 0; A|= (5)/(sqrt(2)\sin (sqrt(2)))]

Therefore, the solution is [MATH: y(x)\sim \bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt gray]{\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2})}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)} +\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this topic, we will use Fourier series to solve boundary value problems with periodic forcing functions.

Content:
As before, we consider a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function [MATH: f(x)], for which the general solution can be written as
[MATH: y=y_c+y_p,]
where [MATH: y_c] solves the homogeneous equation and [MATH: y_p] is a particular solution.

Content:
The main ideas are similar to those of solving IVPs:

Content:
- we choose the correct form of the series for the particular solution [MATH: y_p], and then
- use boundary conditions at the endpoints to determine the constants in the homogeneous part [MATH: y_c] of the solution.

Content:
When [MATH: f(x)] is periodic, we often look for [MATH: y_p] as a Fourier series on a symmetric interval [MATH: [-L,L].]

Content:
Recall that for an equation of the form [MATH: y''+\omega^2 y=f(x)] with no (damping) [MATH: y'] term, the particular solution inherits the parity of [MATH: f(x)]:

Content:
- If [MATH: f] is even, then its Fourier series contains only cosine terms.
- If [MATH: f] is odd, then its Fourier series contains only sine terms.

Content:
For example, consider the boundary value problem
[MATH: y''+5y=f(x)]
on [MATH: [-2,2]], where [MATH: f] is [MATH: 4]-periodic and odd. We want the appropriate Fourier series form for a particular solution [MATH: y_p].

Content:
Because [MATH: f] is [MATH: 4]-periodic on [MATH: [-2,2]], we have [MATH: L=2], so the Fourier basis on this interval is
[MATH: \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).]

Content:
Next, since [MATH: f] is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms. Since the equation has no [MATH: y'] term, the particular solution inherits the same parity and is also odd.

Content:
Therefore, the appropriate form for [MATH: y_p] is a sine series:
[MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{2}\right).]

Content:
Let's see more examples.

Item 2 — Example: Identifying the Form of the Fourier Series For the Solution

on [MATH: [-3,3]], where [MATH: f] is [MATH: 6]-periodic and even. What Fourier-series form is appropriate for a particular solution [MATH: y_p?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Because [MATH: f] is [MATH: 6]-periodic on [MATH: [-3,3]], we have [MATH: L=3], so Fourier series on this interval use the basis
[MATH: \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right).]

Next, since [MATH: f] is even, its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. For a second-order equation with no [MATH: y'] (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an even function.

Therefore, the appropriate form for [MATH: y_p] is a cosine series:
[MATH: y_p(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{3}\right)]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Using Boundary Conditions

Content:
Recall that we are considering a second-order linear differential equation with constant coefficients and forcing function [MATH: f(x)], for which the general solution can be written as
[MATH: y=y_c+y_p,]
where [MATH: y_c] solves the homogeneous equation and [MATH: y_p] is a particular solution.

Content:
There are many types of boundary conditions (including mixed or Robin-type conditions), but in this lesson, we will focus on the two simplest cases:

Content:
- Dirichlet conditions (values of [MATH: y] are specified):
[MATH: y(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=\beta]
- Neumann conditions (values of [MATH: y'] are specified):
[MATH: y'(a)=\alpha
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=\beta]

Content:
A key simplification is possible if we choose our particular solution [MATH: y_p] to satisfy the corresponding homogeneous boundary conditions. For any given [MATH: f(x),] it is always possible to find such a [MATH: y_p].
This drastically simplifies the computations, as the boundary conditions then determine the constants in [MATH: y_c] directly.

Content:
- Dirichlet-type simplification: If we choose the forcing so that
[MATH: y_p(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p(b)=0,]
then
[MATH: y(a)=y_c(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y(b)=y_c(b),]
so we can solve for the constants in [MATH: y_c] using only the homogeneous solution.
- Neumann-type simplification: If we choose the forcing so that
[MATH: y_p'(a)=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_p'(b)=0,]
then
[MATH: y'(a)=y_c'(a)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y'(b)=y_c'(b),]
so the derivative conditions determine the constants in [MATH: y_c] directly.

Content:
Let's see how this works in practice.

Item 6 — Example: Solving BVPs Using Fourier Series

Example Prompt:
Consider the boundary value problem
[MATH: y''+2y=f(x), \qquad y'(0)=0,\quad y'(1)=-5]
where [MATH: f(x)] is [MATH: 2]-periodic and even. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the BVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution [MATH: y_p] of the differential equation.

Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function [MATH: f(x)] is chosen such that the particular solution [MATH: y_p] satisfies [MATH: y_p'(0) = 0] and [MATH: y_p'(1) = 0.]
[MATH: (1)/(xxx)?(1)/(xxx)]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We write the solution as [MATH: y=y_c+y_p], where [MATH: y_c] solves the homogeneous equation and [MATH: y_p] is a particular solution.

First, solve the homogeneous equation [MATH: y''+2y=0.] Its general solution is
[MATH: y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sin(\sqrt{2}x).]

Computing the derivative, we get
[MATH: y'(x)=-A\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sqrt{2}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)+y_p'(x).]

Now, we use the hint. Since [MATH: y_p'(0)=0] and [MATH: y_p'(1)=0], we have
[MATH: y'(0)=y_c'(0)\qquad\text{and}\qquad y'(1)=y_c'(1).]

Next, we apply the boundary conditions.

- Use [MATH: y'(0)=0{:}]
[MATH: y^{′}(0)|= 0 + Bsqrt(2)(1) + y_{p}^{′}(0); 0|= Bsqrt(2) + 0; B|= 0]
So, [MATH: y_c(x)=A\cos(\sqrt{2}x).]
- Use [MATH: y'(1)=-5] with [MATH: B=0{:}]
[MATH: y^{′}(1)|= − Asqrt(2)\sin (sqrt(2)) + y_{p}^{′}(1); − 5|= − Asqrt(2)\sin (sqrt(2)) + 0; A|= (5)/(sqrt(2)\sin (sqrt(2)))]

Therefore, the solution is
[MATH: y(x)\sim \bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt gray]{\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}\sin(\sqrt{2})}\cos(\sqrt{2}x)}
+\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x).]
